options.text: The minimum energy that colliding particles must have for a reaction to occur
The energy stored in the products
The total energy released by a reaction
The energy lost to the surroundings

questions.explanation: Activation energy is the minimum amount of energy that reacting particles must have when they collide in order for a reaction to take place. It is the energy needed to break the bonds in the reactants and start the reaction.

questions.stem: Why do reactions need activation energy even if they are exothermic?

options.text: Because the surroundings must be heated first
Because energy is needed to heat up the products
Because bonds in the reactants must be broken before new bonds can form, and breaking bonds requires energy
Because catalysts need energy to work

questions.explanation: Even in exothermic reactions, the existing bonds in the reactant molecules must first be broken before new bonds can form in the products. This initial bond-breaking step requires an input of energy (the activation energy).

questions.stem: On a reaction profile, where is activation energy shown?

options.text: As the difference between the energy of reactants and products
As the difference between the energy of reactants and the peak (highest point) of the curve
As the distance along the x-axis
As the total area under the curve

questions.explanation: Activation energy is shown on a reaction profile as the energy difference between the reactant energy level and the peak (maximum) of the energy curve. This peak represents the transition state where bonds are partially broken and partially formed.

questions.stem: How does a catalyst affect the activation energy of a reaction?

options.text: It provides an alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy
It increases the activation energy
It does not affect the activation energy
It removes the need for activation energy completely

questions.explanation: A catalyst provides an alternative reaction pathway that has a lower activation energy. This means more particles have enough energy to react when they collide, so the reaction happens faster. The catalyst does not change the overall energy change of the reaction.

questions.stem: A match needs to be struck before it catches fire. What does striking the match provide?

options.text: The activation energy needed to start the combustion reaction
Oxygen for the reaction
A catalyst for the reaction
The products of the reaction

questions.explanation: Striking a match generates friction, which produces heat. This heat provides the activation energy needed to start the exothermic combustion reaction. Once started, the reaction releases enough energy to keep itself going.

questions.stem: If a reaction has a very high activation energy, what would you expect?

options.text: The reaction would be endothermic
The reaction would produce a lot of heat
The reaction would be very slow or not occur at room temperature
The reaction would be very fast at room temperature

questions.explanation: A high activation energy means that very few particles at room temperature have enough energy to react when they collide. The reaction would therefore be very slow or may not occur at all without additional heating or a catalyst.

questions.stem: Does a catalyst change the overall enthalpy change (ΔH) of a reaction?

options.text: No, it only lowers the activation energy but does not change ΔH
Yes, it makes ΔH more positive
Yes, it makes ΔH more negative
Yes, it doubles the value of ΔH

questions.explanation: A catalyst lowers the activation energy by providing an alternative pathway, but it does not change the overall enthalpy change (ΔH) of the reaction. The energy difference between reactants and products remains the same.
